questions.question: Why does `fun <T> isType(x: Any) = x is T` not compile, and what fixes it?
options: `T` needs an upper bound such as `T : Any` before it can be used in an `is` check
Types are erased at runtime, so `T` is unknown; an `inline` function with `reified T` fixes it
`is` checks only work on sealed hierarchies, so `T` must be bounded by a sealed class first
`is` checks need a class literal, so the check has to be written as `x is T::class` instead
questions.explanation: On the JVM, type arguments are erased, so a normal generic function has no runtime value for `T` to check against. An `inline` function with `reified T` is copied into each call site with the real type, so `x is T` and `T::class` work. An upper bound does not stop erasure.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Because `T` is reified, `it is T` is a real runtime check. `only<String>()` keeps "a" and "b", and `List.toString()` prints strings without quotes. `only<Int>()` keeps 1 and 3 only (2.5 is a Double), so the sum is 4.

questions.question: An inline function calls its lambda parameter from inside a `Runnable { }` that it creates. The compiler rejects this. What is the fix, and why?
options: Remove `inline` from the function: lambdas of inline functions can never be used inside other lambdas
Mark the parameter `noinline`: lambdas passed to inline functions can never be captured by other objects
Mark the parameter `reified`: the compiler needs the lambda's runtime type to wrap it in a Runnable
Mark it `crossinline`: it runs in another context, so a non-local `return` from it must be forbidden
questions.explanation: A lambda passed to an inline function may contain a non-local `return`, which only makes sense if it runs directly in the caller's frame. Inside a `Runnable` it may run later or on another thread, so the compiler requires `crossinline`, which forbids non-local returns but still inlines the code. `noinline` also compiles but gives up inlining for that lambda, so it is not the precise fix.

questions.question: A `noinline` lambda parameter of an inline function can be stored in a property or passed to a non-inline function, but a bare `return` inside it is not allowed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `noinline` keeps that lambda as a real function object, so it can be stored or passed on like any value. Because it is no longer inlined into the caller, a non-local `return` is not possible, just as with lambdas passed to regular functions. Labeled returns like `return@label` are still fine.

true

false
UserId(raw=7)

true
7

false
7
questions.explanation: Value classes compare by their underlying value, so two `UserId(7)` are equal. They also get a generated `toString()` in the same style as a data class, `UserId(raw=7)`, not the bare number. At runtime the wrapper is usually erased to `Int`, but the language-level behavior stays the same.

questions.question: For `@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: Int)`, in which uses is a `UserId` boxed into a wrapper object at runtime? Select all that apply.
options: Passed to a parameter of type `Any`
Stored in a `List<UserId>`
Passed to a parameter declared as `UserId`
Held in a `val id: UserId` property
Used as a nullable type, `UserId?`
questions.explanation: The compiler uses the raw `Int` wherever the static type is exactly `UserId`, such as parameters and properties. It must box when the value is used as another type: a generic type argument, `Any`, or a nullable type. So a `List<UserId>` holds boxed objects, which matters on hot paths.

questions.question: What does this contract allow at call sites?
options: The function body is checked at compile time to make sure it really returns true only for non-null input
The call is inlined, and the `s != null` condition replaces the function call at each call site
The compiler inserts a runtime null check and throws if `s` is null when the function returns true
After `if (isValid(s))`, the compiler smart casts `s` to non-null `String` inside the if-block
questions.explanation: `returns(true) implies (s != null)` tells the compiler what a true result means, so callers get the same smart cast they would get from an inline null check. This is how stdlib functions like `isNullOrEmpty()` enable smart casts. The compiler does not verify the contract and adds no runtime check; a wrong contract leads to unsafe code.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: ABend
ABBABBend
ABABdone
ABdone
questions.explanation: Both lambdas are inlined into `test()`, so the bare `return "done"` is a non-local return from `test()` itself. It runs the first time the inner block executes, right after "A" and "B" are printed, so neither loop gets a second pass. Without `inline` this `return` would not compile.

questions.question: When does marking a function `inline` usually NOT help?
options: A large function with no lambda parameters: the body is copied to every call site and nothing is saved
A function that takes a lambda and uses a non-local return, because inlining prevents non-local returns
A function with a `reified` type parameter, because reified parameters are slower than class arguments
A small function that takes a lambda and is called in a hot loop, because inlining blocks JIT optimization
questions.explanation: The main gains of `inline` are avoiding lambda objects and enabling reified types and non-local returns. A big function without lambda parameters gets none of that, only larger bytecode, and the compiler warns that the performance impact is insignificant. Small lambda-taking functions in hot paths are exactly where `inline` helps.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of `@JvmInline value class Email(val value: String)` over `typealias Email = String`?
options: Type safety: a plain `String` cannot be passed where an `Email` is expected
Interop: Java callers see `Email` as its own class, while a typealias is hidden from Java
Validation: a value class automatically rejects strings that are not valid email addresses
Speed: a typealias is boxed at runtime, while a value class always uses the raw `String`
questions.explanation: A typealias is only another name for `String`, so any string can be passed and mix-ups are not caught. A value class is a distinct type at compile time and usually costs nothing extra at runtime. A typealias is not boxed, and validation only happens if you write it in an `init` block.
